The case of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 is that the suit was not maintainable at the instance of the plaintiff, and it is bad for misjoinder and non-joinder of the parties; and also barred by limitation Their further case is that there was no disclosure of the actual value of the cargo in the bill of lading and the defendants as carrier could at best be held liable to pay the plaintiff £ 100.00 per package, as per package limitation clause, for the loss; and that the plaintiff was not entitled to any interest. 

 4. The case of defendant No. 3, Sadharan Bima Corporation is that the plaintiff has no cause of action against this defendant, and no locus standi to sue this defendant inasmuch as the Open Marine Policy and the certificate issued thereunder covering the cargo were taken in the name of Bangladesh Chemical. Industries Corporation A/C Albert David (BD) Ltd. and therefore the BCIC has the right to sue, if at all. In order to examine and scrutinize the claim of the plaintiff, defendant No. 3 requested the plaintiff to submit the original policy and copies of correspondences between the carriers and the plaintiff, but the plaintiff only sent the Marine Insurance Certificate instead of submitting the original policy. Defendent No. 3 also requested the plaintiff to let it know as to whether defendent Nos. 1 and 2 were able to trace the goods and as to the fate of the plaintiff's claim against defendant Nos. 1 and 2. According to defendant No. 3 the short landing of the consignment was not covered under the all risks clause and the defendant did not give any policy giving protection against non-delivery, and that the plaintiff's claim for non-delivery as well as for interest @ 20% per annum of Tk. 10.25,502/- is not payable by defendant No. 3. 

 3. Is the suit bad for misjoinder and non-joinder of parties? 

 8. Is the alleged loss of the plaintiff covered under the policy of insurance when non-delivery was not covered under the policy insurance? 

 10. So far as the present action for non-delivery of the Plaintiff's cargo is concerned the jurisdiction of this Court is not derived from the Letters Patent of 1862 or that of 1865, but from the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act (India) of 1891 and the Court of Admiralty Act, 1861 of England. The latter Act is not on our statute book but it is administered in view of the combined operation of sub-section (2) of section 2 of the colonial Courts of Admiralty Act 1890 of the British Parliament and the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act (India) 1891, the latter Act being revised by the Bangladesh Laws (Revision and Declaration) Act, 1973 (Act VIII of 1973) is now on our statute book. It is true that if the revised Court of Admiralty Act of 1891 is read in isolation then it would not give any idea as to the nature and extent of the Admiralty jurisdiction of this Court, but it is to be read in its historical perspective. Under the Act of 1891 the High Court Division of this Court was declared as the Court of Admiralty. This Court exercises the, same jurisdiction as the High Court of England exercised in 1890 under the Admiralty Court Act of 1861. 

 11. Under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 the High Court of England had jurisdiction to hear and determine any claim relating to carriage of goods in a ship. The instant suit arising out of a claim for non-delivery or the cargo that was to be carried by the ship Nedlloyd Leave is amenable to the jurisdiction of this Court. In view of the above, Issue No.1 is decided in favour of the plaintiff. 

 18. Further case of defendant No.3 is that the suit is bad for non-joinder of necessary parties inasmuch as the BCIC was not impleaded in this case. It has been submitted that the contract of insurance i.e Open Marine Policy was entered into between defendant No. 3 as the Insurer and the BCIC as the insured on account of its various projects and enterprises. The invoice Ext. 1, bill of lading Ext. 3 and Insurance Certificate Ext. 5 indicated that the Corporation was the Insurer under the Policy and it was admitted by P.W. 1 that the open Marine Policy was in the custody of the Corporation. It has been further contended on behalf of defendant No. 1 that the Marine Insurance Policy Ext. 5 is an extended Marine Insurance Policy as contemplated by sub-section (I) of section 2 of the Marine Insurance Act 1906, but it did not coyer the risk of non-delivery, and the risk of non-delivery is not a risk covered under all risks policy, and the plaintiff has also failed to prove that the loss was caused by any maritime peril insured against. 

 19. On 30.3.82 after the argument for defendant No. 3 was concluded the plaintiff filed an application for bringing on record a copy of the Open Insurance Policy. To meet the defendant's objective that the Insurance Policy did not contain the signature of the authorised Officer of the Corporation on all the pages and it was not a stamped document the plaintiff filed on the following day the original Open Marine Policy. Defendant No. 3 admitted, the document filed on 31.3.82 to be the original one. The Open Marine Insurance Policy at page 6 shows that it covers risks of non-delivery as well. 

 22. On behalf of defendant No. 3 it has been urged that by the Marine Insurance Certificate (Ext. 5) the consignment was covered only against "All Risks, Rail and/or Inland conveyance including war strike, riot and civil commotion" and not against non-delivery. In view of the wide expressions of the risk clause which includes rail &/ or Inland conveyance and that the Open Marine insurance Policy covers non-delivery as well the contention of the insurance company is rejected. Issue No. 8 is decided against defendant No. 3. 

 The plaintiff is entitled to realise the value of the cargo from the carrier and the insurer, but as it has failed to substantiate its claim for 20% interest per annum on the value of the goods non-delivered I reject that claim.  In above terms issue Nos. 6 and 7 are decided in favour of the plaintiff.
